pr_comments: Isn't python 3.11 exhibiting the correct behavior?

> Isn't python 3.11 exhibiting the correct behavior?

No, see the example in #49649 .  It is preventing subclassing `DataFrame` as a `Generic`.

I think what happened here is that python 3.11 added an `__iter__()` method to the class representing the type of the `Generic`, so we see that type as being "list like".  Then internally, the typing module assigns an attribute to the instance, which we then complain about.  Prior to 3.11, the `__iter__()` method wasn't there, so we were OK.
Ah OK thanks for the explanation. If you replaced `Gen[T]` in your test with `list[T]` what would your expectation be? I think we should add that as a test as well

> Ah OK thanks for the explanation. If you replaced `Gen[T]` in your test with `list[T]` what would your expectation be? I think we should add that as a test as well

Before seeing that message, I updated the test to more explicitly test the case of subclassing a `DataFrame` .  So I'm not sure if we need to test `list[T]` .  

The issue is that when you instantiate the subclass that is `Generic`, the typing module creates an attribute on the class and we issue a warning:
```text
C:\Anaconda3\envs\pandas-dev311\Lib\typing.py:1253: UserWarning: Pandas doesn't allow columns to be created via a new attribute name - see https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/indexing.html#attribute-access
  result.__orig_class__ = self
```

Here `result` is a `DataFrame`, and `self` is the `_GenericAlias` .
Perf?

> Perf?

Have to assume that the difference between doing `isinstance(obj, (str, bytes))` and `isinstance(obj, (str, bytes, _GenericAlias))` is minimal.  And that our benchmarks won't see the difference.
I'm sure it will be small, but this is a function that we've gone out of our way to optimize to the gills

> I'm sure it will be small, but this is a function that we've gone out of our way to optimize to the gills

So what's the methodology to do the comparison?  In CI?  Locally?

And if there is a hit, then what do we do about it?

> So what's the methodology to do the comparison? In CI? Locally?

usually show some before/after results with `%timeit` in a few cases chosen using your best judgement

> > So what's the methodology to do the comparison? In CI? Locally?
> 
> usually show some before/after results with `%timeit` in a few cases chosen using your best judgement

OK, so I did this test
BEFORE
```python
%timeit inference.is_list_like(set([1,2,3]))
572 ns ± 14.4 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1,000,000 loops each)
```

AFTER
```python
%timeit inference.is_list_like(set([1,2,3]))
592 ns ± 12 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1,000,000 loops each)
```

I tested a `set` because it is the last thing checked in `is_list_like`, so we know the new test is always executed.  This is with python 3.8 on my Windows machine.

Open to other tests to try.
thanks

issue_context.title: BUG: warning from typing library if you subclass a DataFrame using Generic with python 3.11
issue_context.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

T = TypeVar("T")

class MyDataFrame(pd.DataFrame, Generic[T]):
    ...

def func() -> MyDataFrame[int]:
    return MyDataFrame[int]({"foo": [1, 2, 3]})

x = func()
print(x)
```


### Issue Description

With pandas 1.5.1 and python 3.10, the code above gives no warning at runtime.

With pandas 1.5.1 and python 3.11, you get a warning from the typing library at runtime:
```text
C:\Anaconda3\envs\pandasstubs311\Lib\typing.py:1253: UserWarning: Pandas doesn't allow columns to be created via a new attribute name - see https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/indexing.html#attribute-access
  result.__orig_class__ = self
```

We have testing code in pandas-stubs that uses this, because it was reported by the people developing the `pandera` library.


### Expected Behavior

No warning.

We're doing something in pandas that doesn't allow a `Generic` subclass to be created with python 3.11.

comments:
Seems like `is_list_like()` is not handling a generic alias correctly:
```python
import pandas as pd

from pandas._libs import lib
import sys

is_list_like = lib.is_list_like


from typing import TypeVar, Generic

T = TypeVar("T")


class Base:
    def __init__(self, x: int):
        self._x = x


class Gen(Base, Generic[T]):
    ...


fooc = Gen[float]
print(type(fooc))
print(sys.version)
print("pandas version ", pd.__version__)
print(is_list_like(fooc))
```
With python 3.10, output is
```text
<class 'typing._GenericAlias'>
3.10.4 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Mar 30 2022, 08:38:02) [MSC v.1916 64 bit (AMD64)]
pandas version  1.5.1
False
```
With python 3.11, output is
```text
<class 'typing._GenericAlias'>
3.11.0 | packaged by conda-forge | (main, Oct 25 2022, 06:12:32) [MSC v.1929 64 bit (AMD64)]
pandas version  1.5.1
True
```

Hi everyone, I'm getting a warning `UserWarning: Pandas doesn't allow columns to be created via a new attribute name` when assigning a dictionary as an attribute to a class inheriting from `DataFrame`.
I have not found this issue being reported.

Version checks: python version 3.10.7, pandas 1.5.3

Example:
```python
import pandas as pd

class MyClass(pd.DataFrame):
    def __init__(self, dct_frame, dct_settings):
        pd.DataFrame.__init__(self, dct_frame)
        self.settings = dct_settings


mc = MyClass({'a': [1,2], 'b': [3,4]}, {'plot_style': 'param_per_chanenl'})
```

Warning message:
```
UserWarning: Pandas doesn't allow columns to be created via a new attribute name - see https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/indexing.html#attribute-access
  self.settings = dct_settings
```

Is there a way to combat this? Or should I find another way of structuring my class to avoid this?
I'm an amateur and don't know how to structure a comment in an issue thread properly, but didn't know where else to ask, as I'm not finding discussions on this, so I want to apologize for bothering.

Because pandas allows referring to columns as an attribute, you can't add attributes to a subclass.  You can store your additional attributes in `Dataframe.attrs`

The following should work:
```python
import pandas as pd

class MyClass(pd.DataFrame):
    def __init__(self, dct_frame, dct_settings):
        pd.DataFrame.__init__(self, dct_frame)
        self.attrs["settings"] = dct_settings
```
Thanks for the lightning fast response! It did not flash the warning when creating string attributes in the subclass, but did for a dict attribute. I will follow your suggestion.
